analysis.title: AI's 2008 Moment: Jefferies Sees "Massive Capital Destruction" As Two Cash-Burning Labs Owe Half Of A $2.3 Trillion Backlog
key_insights: Jefferies' Chris Wood (Asia Maxima 4Q26, 'Reverberating tremors') says the most likely longer-term market outcome of the AI story is massive capital destruction in the US, with market share going to cheaper open-source Chinese large language models.
Chinese models now compete on quality as well as price. Wood quotes Kimi K3 as competing at the frontier with an estimated 95% of the performance of Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.

Top Chinese models processed 76.12 trillion tokens on OpenRouter in the week ended Sept 27, up from 4.37 trillion in late April and more than 5x the 14.2 trillion for top US models. In late July the count was 36.39 trillion vs 7.39 trillion. OpenRouter is one aggregator and skews toward price-sensitive developers.
Silicon Data's LLM Token Expenditure Index has fallen 52% from its late-May peak to an all-time low of $0.98 per million tokens.
Token demand is up roughly 18x since December per Goldman, but demand for expensive frontier models appears to have plateaued. Hyperscaler realized ROIC has slid from 40% to 25%.

Wood sees a 2008 real estate credit angle. Of about $2.3tn aggregate contracted backlog across Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Oracle, about half is owed by OpenAI and Anthropic, neither of which is profitable. Backlog (RPO) reached $2.34tn at end of 2Q26, up 186% ($1.52tn) in four quarters.

Jefferies tech analysts estimate the two frontier labs were roughly 45% of Google Cloud Platform revenue and 25% of Microsoft Azure in 2Q26. Their AWS share is expected to rise from 6% to 12-18% in 3Q26.

Goldman estimates Amazon, Microsoft and Google need about $1.0tn of revenue in 2028-30 to earn a 15% ROIC on 2026-27 AI capex, about 59% of their combined $1.69tn cloud backlog. The article argues that backlog not owed by the two labs would fall well short of that hurdle, though the comparison is not like-for-like because Wood's figure includes Oracle.

The five hyperscalers including Oracle have issued $229bn of bonds this year vs $108bn in all of 2025, and are the largest investment-grade issuer by category. Amazon, Alphabet and Meta spreads are up 13-16bps since early June, and Wood says hyperscaler funding demand now competes with the federal government.

Off-balance-sheet exposure: Moody's counted $662bn of not-yet-commenced data center leases at the top five in February (vs $152bn at end-2023). A Nikkei study put hidden debt at $1.65tn at end 2Q26 vs about $1.35tn on-balance-sheet debt. ZeroHedge's own tracker shows $3.8tn as of Sept 30, up $700bn from June 30.

Albert Edwards (SocGen) compares the AI boom to the 1997 Asian crisis. Utilization-adjusted total factor productivity is just below zero despite the capex boom, and the mechanism is cheap capital misallocated until lenders stop lending.

Earnings are stellar (S&P 500 3Q26 EPS expected +30.2% YoY, IT +65.1%) but cash is not. Big-four hyperscaler free cash flow fell from $60bn in 4Q25 to $7bn in 2Q26 and is expected at -$13bn in 3Q26 as quarterly capex heads to $200bn. Consensus capex is $723bn this year and $993bn in 2027.

Wood argues mark-to-market gains on AI stakes explain all of the hyperscaler earnings growth. Annualised earnings rose $222bn YoY to $581bn in the four quarters to 2Q26, while other non-operating income rose $224bn. The article calls this circular, since hyperscalers invest in labs that buy compute from them.

S&P 500 reported EPS has grown an annualized 18% over three years vs 5% for NIPA nonfinancial corporate profits. The last comparable divergence was the dot-com peak (EPS +10% annualized in the three years to 3Q00 vs NIPA -8%). Wood calls this financial engineering.

Wood reads last month's agreement by Amodei, Altman and Musk to slow frontier AI development as a possible regulatory moat or cartel, possibly with a plan to ban open-source Chinese models. Trump rejected the request. Zuckerberg rejected it and Meta is up 18% since.

A Stanford/Together AI study ('Intelligence per Watt') finds small language models have 50-85% lower energy and compute costs than data-center LLMs, which Wood says could reduce demand for GPUs and centralized cloud if firms run AI on-prem.

Wood's base case is that the US share of world market cap peaked at 67.2% of MSCI ACWI on 24 Dec 2024 and closed last quarter at 64.2%. His prescription is to own picks and shovels (chipmakers) rather than hyperscalers, and he says credit spreads of AI borrowers must be monitored for any sign investors are unwilling to fund AI capex.

market_movers.rationale: Meta rejected calls for an AI slowdown and is up 18% since. Its Muse app launched 8 September, but Hunterbrook data show daily net user gains down 62.4% from the September surge.

sector_views.rationale: Wood expects capital destruction as returns fade, free cash flow turns negative and capex is debt-funded.
Picks and shovels book hyperscaler capex as revenue, which works as long as buyers keep buying.

earnings_insights: S&P 500 3Q26 EPS is expected to rise 30.2% YoY (consensus expectation), with IT up 65.1%, per Wood.
Four big hyperscalers' annualised earnings rose $222bn YoY to $581bn in the four quarters to 2Q26 (reported), while other non-operating income rose $224bn, per Wood's analysis.
Hyperscaler aggregate free cash flow was $60bn in 4Q25 and $7bn in 2Q26 (reported), with 3Q26 expected at -$13bn (estimate).
Consensus capex for the big four is $723bn in 2026 and $993bn in 2027 (estimates).

macro_indicators.interpretation: Earnings growth is strong but the article argues it is driven by non-cash mark-to-market gains.
Tech earnings carry the S&P growth rate.
Wider spreads suggest AI funding demand is competing with Treasury issuance.

tension_points.bull_case: Earnings are stellar (S&P 3Q26 EPS +30.2%, IT +65.1%). Contracted backlog of $2.34tn is read as proof of demand, and Goldman sees the contracted revenue as comfort against its $1.0tn hurdle. Collapsing token prices keep compute demand growing under the Jevons Paradox.
tension_points.bear_case: Roughly half the backlog is owed by cash-burning OpenAI and Anthropic. Hyperscaler free cash flow is falling toward negative and ROIC is slipping from 40% to 25%. Earnings growth is explained by mark-to-market gains on AI stakes, and capex is increasingly debt-funded.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Credit spreads of AI-related borrowers widening or investors becoming unwilling to finance AI capex, with data center securitisation the area Wood says to monitor.

theme_stances.key_argument: Collapsing token prices and cheaper Chinese open-source models make LLMs hard to profit from, leaving debt-funded data centers exposed to cash-burning tenants.
